rationale: C10 plausibly supplied a material drafting template. Both memoranda reject a federal-pay measure by first identifying fair and equitable treatment relative to private employment as the governing principle, then arguing that the bill disregards that principle, aggravates pay disparities, imposes unjustified federal costs, and harms the broader economy. The child adapts this framework from general federal salary increases to a locality-specific wage-board exception. C20 and C21 share the narrower structural objection to creating preferential or uncoordinated pay treatment for one employee group, but their language and overall argumentative sequence are less closely aligned.

shared_material.child_excerpt: rates of pay for 673,000 federal wage board employees shall conform...with private rates of pay in the immediate vicinity... This principle is sound. It insures federal employees a fair wage.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: Federal employees have the right to expect fair and equitable wage treatment...in relation to employees in private business.
shared_material.explanation: Both articulate substantially the same public/private wage-comparability principle as the central standard for judging the bill.

shared_material.parent_excerpt: These bills disregard that fundamental principle.
shared_material.explanation: Distinctively parallel language introduces the conclusion that the proposed pay legislation violates the previously stated compensation principle.

shared_material.child_excerpt: why should the Government pay a much higher hourly wage rate than do fair-minded private employers in the Portsmouth area?
shared_material.parent_excerpt: it has not been demonstrated that generally the present conditions of Federal employment are out of line with those...working in private industry.
shared_material.explanation: Both test the proposed federal compensation against comparable private-sector pay and reject increases unsupported by that comparison.

shared_material.child_excerpt: the Government would be departing from sound principle and business practice and would be unsettling the economy
shared_material.parent_excerpt: they would contribute unnecessarily to existing and incipient inflationary pressures in our national economy.
shared_material.explanation: Both extend the pay-equity objection into a broader economic argument against government-driven wage increases.
